title: Doctors in Congress used to lean Republican – the 120th Congress marks a historic shift
paragraphs: The 120th Congress, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, will have 20 physicians as members, along with twice that number of members who have other professional health backgrounds.

This physician class will make history for including the most Democratic physicians in a single Congress – 11 – in American history – a marked shift from the Republican dominance of previous physician members. These Democratic physicians made their professional expertise and their health policy ideas centerpieces of their campaigns, and now they have the opportunity to advance their health policy agendas.

I am a political scientist who studies the partisan politics of health and health policy in the U.S. While physicians have long shaped American health policy, the physician class elected to the upcoming Congress is the most Democratic in the modern era.

The Democratic physician class in the Senate includes South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Andrews made reproductive health and rural healthcare access core tenets of her campaign. For instance, her campaign website stressed that “As a doctor and a mom, I’ve cared for women in some of the most difficult moments of their lives. … I’ll fight to: Restore the protections of Roe v. Wade, Guarantee access to contraception and infertility care, Expand maternal health services, especially in rural areas.”

In the House of Representatives, the Democratic physician class includes California’s Richard Pan, also a pediatrician. Pan’s campaign website, which featured many pictures and references to his physician background and stressed the importance of holding “RFK accountable for endangering Americans” – referring to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – as well as fighting to lower prescription drug costs, preventing the continued withering of the Affordable Care Act and banning prior authorization.

Other Democratic medical doctors who will be serving in the 120th Congress include two newly elected members in the House, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey and Amish Shah of Arizona, in addition to six returning representatives. Newly elected to the Senate alongside Andrews is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, an epidemiologist with a medical doctorate.

Beyond Congress, Democratic medical doctors will also serve as governors – with Amy Acton newly elected in Ohio and Josh Green reelected in Hawaii – as well as in numerous state legislative positions.

Physicians have played important roles in shaping American politics and health policies, back to the nation’s founding. For instance, Pennsylvania’s Dr. Benjamin Rush, an early public health advocate who led the city of Philadelphia through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793, was the only person with a medical degree to sign the Declaration of Independence.

Since the late 1980s, the number of physicians serving in Congress has increased substantially term over term. My colleagues and I have documented this rise, as well as how physician members of the House have influenced policy.

We found that physician members of the House were more active and effective in enacting health policy than other members. Physician members were more likely to sponsor health legislation, and their health bills advanced further in the legislative process. This was true for physicians from both parties, both on and off congressional health-related committees.

Since at least 1973, when our data begin, physician House members’ congressional voting behaviors and their health policies have been more conservative than other members on average, even those of their own parties. For example, we found that physician members were more likely to sponsor bills related to curbing abortion access, repealing the ACA and protecting private sector physician autonomy.

However, one of the most striking changes we observed was the shift from the Republican dominance of physician members of Congress to the steadily increasing number of Democratic physicians elected since 2015. That year, there were just two Democratic physicians in Congress, but the 119th Congress – 2025-2027 – has six Democratic physicians. The upcoming Congress will nearly double that amount, with the largest class of Democratic members with medical doctorates in American history.

It will be the first Democratic physician majority since 1995, during the 103rd Congress, when two out of the three physician House members were Democrats. Before 1995, physician members were much rarer, but the majority of them were Republicans. Between 1995 and 2023, 80% of physician members were Republicans.
These partisan changes reflect the broader partisan shifts within the medical community itself.
For most of the 20th century, the majority of physicians – both in Congress and more generally as a group – were Republicans. The American Medical Association was largely a conservative organization.
The party loyalties of today’s physician class mirror the slowly shifting demographics of physicians as a group.
Since the 1970s – and especially since the 1990s – medical school applicants and new physicians have become more diverse in terms of gender, race and ethnicity.

These groups tend to identify as Democrats at higher rates, though medicine as a field continues to be dominated by white men. Additionally, becoming a physician obviously requires getting an undergraduate and a professional degree, but higher educational attainment alone has also become increasingly related to Democratic support.
Beyond these more glacial demographic changes, three Trump-era events have shaped the political mobilization of Democratic physicians.

First, the partisan politics of COVID-19 and especially the politicization of the COVID-19 vaccine, has been associated with decreasing trust in medicine and science from Republican-aligned voters and an increase in physicians’ Democratic support.

Second, the elevation of Kennedy as HHS secretary, whose own vaccine skepticism has long run contrary to medical science and the advice of physicians, further pitted many physicians against the Republican Party.

Finally, the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned the Constitutional right to abortion, also appears to have politically mobilized many OB-GYNs and other women’s health professionals in response to threats to the care they provide and their professional livelihoods.
All these factors have contributed to a new physician class in Congress that is more Democratic and liberal in their health policy views than previous years.

Ultimately, what this difference means for future public policy remains to be seen. However, if politicians’ campaign priorities portend their legislative activity, there may be a more active push than Congress has ever seen for health reforms related to reproductive healthcare, rural health, prescription drug pricing, bans on prior authorization requirements by health insurers and maybe even Medicare for all.

title: California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later
paragraphs: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.
As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results.

In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate.

As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs.
We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at.

For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%.
This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain.

The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own.

Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own.
In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027.
The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists.

In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero.
More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run.

Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage?

We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures.

We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones.

For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period.
But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose.

How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones.

A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses.

First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%.

That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains.

Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage.

For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear.

title: Prepaid electricity can make bills more predictable, but not necessarily more affordable
paragraphs: The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it. If the tank ran out, there was no heat in the home, and we had to pay extra for an emergency refill and for someone to relight the pilot. A full tank of oil could last up to a month and a half – but only if we kept the heat at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) when we were home and cut it off when we went to work.
Where I live now, in Pennsylvania, we use natural gas and pay afterward, based on our use. It amounts to $200 to $400 monthly – and lets us keep our heat around 70 F (21 C).

Prepaying for heat in Massachusetts certainly made me more aware of how much heating a home cost, but it didn’t make energy cheaper or help me live according to modern standards. Instead, I got used to wearing my winter coat indoors. This is still a concern for many: As winter 2026 approached, some families in Maine that have oil heat had their kids sleep in snowsuits to use less fuel and keep costs down.

Most electricity companies bill for energy already used – like the natural gas company I have in Pennsylvania. But in Maryland, Baltimore Gas and Electric is proposing a prepaid electricity program, similar to my Massachusetts oil setup.

As an energy affordability researcher studying how people change their habits to use less energy when it’s expensive, the real question for me is what this type of payment system would mean for customers. Helping households manage electricity bills is different from ensuring they can afford to use enough energy at home to keep themselves safe.

BGE, which serves approximately 1.3 million electric customers, asked Maryland Public Service Commission members to approve a prepaid program for customers in July 2026. The company says this would help people keep a better handle on their energy spending.

Rather than getting a monthly bill, customers who opted into the plan would make an initial $40 payment toward future electricity use. They could then monitor their power usage and get alerts when balances run low.

The utility’s vice president of regulatory policy and strategy, John Frain, told the Maryland Public Service Commission that prepaid customers wouldn’t have to pay security deposits to open new accounts and wouldn’t have to worry about late payment or reconnection fees if service were disconnected because they weren’t able to pay their bills.

For customers with unpaid balances of up to $1,000, the company would have 25% of each prepayment applied to previous debts and 75% go toward future electricity costs. The company expects to save a yet-undetermined amount of money on collection efforts.
Consumer advocates warn that prepaid billing could cause problems for customers while making life easier for the utility company.
For instance, people on fixed incomes, such as Social Security, could experience increased mental stress because of frequent fears their electricity might be cut off.

They also might make significant changes in their lifestyles: A 2014 study in New Zealand found customers who prepaid for their electricity rationed their own power by, for instance, turning on an electric water heater only every third day and taking cold showers on other days.

Because Maryland prepaid customers would pay the same electricity rates as everyone else, any bill savings would likely come from living without many of the basic services electricity brings to modern life.

The company’s response to this concern is that while customers whose balance gets to zero will be disconnected – as soon as the next day – they’ll have an easier time getting reconnected. Once people add $15 to their account, power can be restored in less than 30 minutes.

But even short disconnections can cause big problems. For people dependent on electric-powered medical devices, such as breathing equipment or home dialysis machines, getting disconnected can injure or kill them. Without the power to charge a phone or power a Wi-Fi router, some people may have trouble getting alerts about their balance or making payments to turn their electricity back on.

Under traditional billing, Maryland law gives customers protections against rapid disconnections. When people are late paying their bills, utilities have to notify them of the overdue balance and give them at least 14 days to pay before cutting off power – a period during which they can still use electricity.
This delay gives people a chance to make payment arrangements and seek financial assistance, such as from the state’s Office of Home Energy Programs.
Applying to that office allows customers to request an additional 55-day reprieve from disconnection, which can help families stay connected during extreme weather events.
In August 2019, BGE conducted a trial run of the prepaid system with 527 customers.

An independent analysis found that power disconnections were often shorter – five hours on average – for prepaid customers than for customers who were billed later for the power they used, whose power was off for an average of 9.4 days. But 10% of prepaid customers had their power cut off at some point during the test period, compared with just 1% of those in the traditional billing program.

The trial run generated some positive outcomes for customers: 61% of the participants said they had better control over their energy bills by being able to decide when and how much to prepay, and 34% said the program’s feature of progressively paying off overdue bills helped them.
However, 41% of participants left before the program formally ended in November 2020. Among those who left, one-third didn’t like making frequent payments, and 23% felt their energy cost more.
BGE told Maryland officials that the prepaid program is “not intended as a cost-savings program for customers.”
The company says its prepay program offers customers online tools to monitor their energy use and the option to make payments when it’s financially convenient.

title: The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history
paragraphs: The sold-out crowd at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida revived its “Gator bait” cheer at its 2026 season opener.

When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”

The decision to bring back the popular cheer reversed a ban imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide reckoning over race that followed the murder of George Floyd.

Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it remained “meaningful to the Gator family.” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has not publicly identified who formally authorized its return.

The controversy surrounding this chant has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to embrace a tradition that risks making some students and alumni feel less welcome on campus.

As an environmental and cultural historian and author of “Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.

The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “certain exhalation” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.
White plantation owners eagerly took up this racist theory because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.

After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to reassert white supremacy. Alongside disenfranchisement, Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism, they promoted stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans.

One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the intimidation, exclusion and violence that African Americans routinely faced during this period.

It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A bestselling photograph bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.

The epithet soon spread through newspapers, postcards, editorial cartoons, songs and films. Ostensibly humorous images of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.

Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of historical debate. But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades.

As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a 1939 newspaper account of a home game against Georgia Tech.

When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”

While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” remained a recognizable racial slur. By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a regular fixture at Florida football games.

The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. Like most Southern universities, the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, enrolling its first African American law student, George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived four years later, and the football team remained segregated until 1968.

Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the Confederate battle flag on his players’ helmets before the Gator Bowl.

As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual “Old South” weekend that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a mock execution of Union General William T. Sherman and a secession proclamation.

When the student newspaper surveyed the campus in 1968 about whether to continue playing “Dixie” – the unofficial anthem of the Confederate States of America – at football games, 83% of students supported the practice. But the majority of Black students surveyed opposed it. “Dixie” remained a game-day staple until 1973.

By the late 20th century, most Florida fans no longer understood “Gator bait” through the lens of Jim Crow-era racial stereotypes. Decades of use at football games had transformed the chant into a symbol of school spirit and athletic success.

No individual played a larger role in that transformation than Lawrence Wright, the hard-hitting safety who helped lead Florida to its first national championship. Wright, who is African American, did not invent the cheer, as is often claimed, but he helped elevate it to iconic status. Following Florida’s victory over rival Florida State in 1995, he famously rallied fans with the refrain, “If you ain’t a Gator, you must be Gator bait.”

When the Gators became national champions the next season, the chant became even more deeply enshrined in Florida football culture. For most fans, “Gator bait” came to symbolize pride in the university rather than anything connected to the phrase’s earlier racist history.
Yet that history never disappeared.

title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
paragraphs: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

The same type of species, Cladosporium sphaerospermum, has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.

I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early in my Ph.D. research when I read a 2019 study from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.

Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties.

Scientists think allomelanin is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers.

Allomelanin has another remarkable property. My colleagues showed in 2021 that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity.

These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, including toxic ones, a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from natural fungi or whether it is synthesized in our lab.
In a recent study published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?

Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called organophosphorus compounds. They block an enzyme the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.

Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.

Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A 2026 analysis estimated that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.

Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well.

Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.

To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters made of a metal called zirconium. Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.

Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of metal-organic frameworks, which are among the most studied materials for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.
We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land.

For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.

Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.
This reaction usually needs alkaline conditions, which have a high pH and are the opposite of acidic – for example, baking soda dissolved in water is alkaline.

Water alone breaks down the trapped molecules far too slowly, over weeks or months. Alkaline conditions supply hydroxide, a negatively charged relative of water that is drawn to the molecule’s most dangerous bond and helps the zirconium snap it in minutes. In the lab, that means we add a liquid chemical to make the conditions alkaline, but doing so isn’t practical for a soldier’s jacket or a farmworker’s mask. Instead, we attached alkaline chemical groups directly to the particle surfaces.

We then took advantage of another property of melanin: It absorbs light and turns it into heat. Under a bright lamp for five minutes, the particles broke down about 10 times more of the stand-in chemical than they did in the dark. Simply heating the samples in the dark had a much smaller effect, which suggests light does more than warm the particles.

Our work has important limits. We tested a chemical surrogate in laboratory vials rather than using live nerve agents or agricultural pesticides floating in the air. We also have not yet woven these particles into commercial textiles. Our immediate next steps are to evaluate the material against the specific pesticides farmworkers encounter daily and to refine the particle coating process.

Getting the material into fabrics may be more straightforward than it sounds. Synthetic melanin naturally adheres to textile fibers without needing chemical glues, and our research group has previously demonstrated that synthetic melanins could act as sustainable fabric dyes.

In the future, we hope this work can help develop lightweight gloves, masks and uniforms that continuously destroy toxic chemicals on contact as people work in the sun. Zirconium is a common and relatively inexpensive metal, and each particle uses only a small amount, though we haven’t evaluated what the cost of making these materials at a larger scale could be.

title: What was the first animal that ever lived on Earth?
paragraphs: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Imagine climbing into a time machine and setting the dial for when the very first animal was alive. You would need to travel really, really far back in time.

You would blow past the dinosaurs, which showed up about 230 million years ago. Keep going and you’d pass coil-shelled ammonites that swam in the oceans starting 450 million years ago, and then trilobites, armored animals that scuttled across the seafloor more than 520 million years ago. Further still, around 558 million years ago, you would meet Dickinsonia, a tiny, flat, ribbed oval only a few millimeters thick that looks more like a squashed pancake than any animal you know.
And even Dickinsonia was almost certainly not the first animal.
We are biologists who study single-celled life called protists. How complex life such as human beings showed up in the first place is one of the major questions in our field.
Honestly, nobody can name the first animal, but there are many clues about what it was probably like.
If we asked you what an animal is, you might say something that moves, eats and reproduces. The trouble is that plenty of nonanimals do all three.
For instance, single-celled amoebae crawl, hunt and swallow their prey whole – and they are not animals at all!

Biologists define an animal as an organism made of many cells that stick together, communicate and divide up the work of growing, eating and moving. Different types of cells specialize to do different jobs, and they all work together as one organism. And when animals eat, they take in outside material instead of making their own food from sunlight the way plants do.
Notice what is not on that list: Legs. Eyes. A brain. A mouth. That matters for what comes next.

SpongeBob SquarePants is a cartoon version of a real animal, the sea sponge. Real sponges do not wear square pants; they don’t even move around. They sit anchored to the seafloor, pumping seawater through thousands of tiny holes and straining out bacteria to eat. They have no brain, no heart and no muscles.

But sponges are still animals, and scientists often think of them as the simplest ones. Part of what makes them so interesting is a type of cell they have called choanocytes. Each choanocyte has a whiplike tail ringed by tiny fingerlike projections that trap food.

Choanocytes look almost exactly like choanoflagellates, free-living, single-celled organisms that are the closest living relatives of animals. Watching a colony of choanoflagellates feed together is about as close as you can get to seeing the doorway between single-celled life and animal life.

Imagine climbing down the animal tree of life going backward in time. You can start with animals alive today, which would be the leaves of the tree. Branches join where you encounter ancestors shared by different groups. Follow them far enough, and they all meet at a common ancestor of living animals. Scientists disagree about which groups belong on each side of that deepest branching point.

Some studies put sponges alone on one side of that fork, with every other living animal group, including us, on the other. Other studies put comb jellies in that position. In that case, these shimmering, jellylike ocean swimmers would occupy one side, while sponges and all other animals would occupy the other. This is what scientists mean when they describe either group as having “branched off first.”

It is important to remember that “branched off first” does not mean “unchanged.” Sponges, comb jellies and humans have all been evolving for the same amount of time, since our shared ancestor lived. Each lineage has followed its own evolutionary path, which over time has led to the great diversity of animals we see today, such as worms, insects, crabs and primates. Today’s sponges and comb jellies may therefore look very different from that common ancestor, making it difficult to picture what the first animal looked like.
Comparative biology can take us only so far.

Fossils are another source of information, but they show just a very narrow window into the past. Fossilization turns living material into stone, a process that works far better on hard parts such as shells, teeth and bones than on soft, squishy bodies. Because early animals were probably soft and small, they were likely easily erased from the record.

Also, fossilization works better in some kinds of environments than others. For example, muddy lake bottoms can bury dead organisms, protecting their remains from rapid decay so they have time to fossilize; any remains on wave-battered shores may wash away before they can fossilize.

Another line of evidence now available to scientists is genetic information. Genes, encoded in DNA strands inside every living organism, provide an instruction manual for how to build that creature. Cells copy that DNA and pass it on – a process that’s been going on for billions of years, generation after generation.

This genetic information accumulates slight changes over time, which scientists call mutations. It is the very existence of mutations that allows evolution – how life changes over time – to happen. This process is what generated the diversity of life you see today.

By studying the structure and architecture of DNA, as well as how it gets passed along, scientists can mathematically assemble family trees that extend very deep into the past. These family trees can help scientists make surprisingly good guesses about when and where an animal first arose. A creature’s genes hint at what it could possibly do.
Biologist Iñaki Ruiz-Trillo and his colleagues use a smartphone analogy that we find particularly useful when talking about the origin of animals.
A smartphone was not invented from scratch. Cameras, telephones, computers and the internet were all invented separately first. The innovation was combining them into a single piece of equipment.

title: How a Pittsburgh-born umpire painted baseball history onto the ball itself
paragraphs: Baseballs are charismatic objects. It is no accident that the narrative spine of novelist Don DeLillo’s magnum opus of 20th-century American life, “Underworld,” involves the ownership of the baseball from the “shot heard ’round the world” – the ninth-inning home run New York Giants slugger Bobby Thomson hit to beat the Brooklyn Dodgers for the 1951 National League pennant. A lot of Americana has been projected onto the surface of a baseball.

But the surface of a baseball is not typically a canvas. The 26 or so square inches of area, created when two pieces of leather are connected with 108 red stitches, are awkward surfaces on which to draw. And most of the time, the only thing people want drawn on baseballs is a signature from an admired player.
But that’s not how George Sosnak saw them.

Born in Pittsburgh in 1924, Sosnak worked as a minor league umpire starting in his 30s, but he became better known as a self-taught artist over the subsequent four decades. Each baseball offered Sosnak at least four spaces to fill with images of players, team insignia or text recounting playing statistics or triumphs, all meticulously rendered in India ink.
An ongoing exhibit at the Westmoreland Museum of American Art features over 60 of the approximately 800 balls he finished painting in his lifetime – he began painting nearly 3,000 balls.

Sosnak’s creations are often colorful, depicting players in action, with facts about them or their games written alongside. Many of the baseballs function as miniature stories, a spherical, secular altarpiece that tells the story of a key game or season.
His “Pittsburgh Pirates, 1978” ball features Harold “Pie” Traynor, Bill Mazeroski and Roberto Clemente.

Traynor and Clemente had both died in 1972, the year Mazeroski retired, and the three never played on a single team together. Depicting three of Sosnak’s most legendary hometown Pirates together created a kind of pantheon, with the timeless image of Clemente finishing his swing juxtaposed with the specific moment Mazeroski raised his hat while circling the bases after hitting the home run that won the 1960 World Series.

Sosnak’s scenes often involve these juxtapositions, using the raised seams and the uneven leather strips to both separate and connect moments for artistic effect. He even depicted something other than baseball itself on the balls, including other sports. But his main focus was on using the spherical leather canvas to memorialize the moments and people that mattered to Sosnak – and to fellow fans who commissioned the balls. He often used such detail – spectators in Forbes Field represented by tiny ink dashes – that magnifying glasses are required to fully appreciate the nuances.

Sosnak linked the American folk art tradition with the talismanic nature of an actual baseball. Unlike the case in most other professional sports, some fans come away from baseball games with balls as souvenirs — whether they were hit as home runs or foul balls, or just tossed into the crowd by players.

Baseballs are disposable – most balls last only a few pitches, so around 100 balls are used in every professional game – and yet they become treasured relics when caught. Sosnak’s painted balls combine these tensions: You can hold one in your hand, visualizing its past while touching the otherwise disposable object that was imparted meaning only through the triumph.

title: Paid sick leave laws are no guarantee for Philly’s immigrant restaurant workers
paragraphs: What do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day.

There is no federal right to paid sick leave. However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide, requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees.
In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck.
For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy.

I study restaurant work, an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born. Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala.

I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez.

Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015. During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act, a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees.

A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees.
What I found, though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers.

Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “reasonable documentation” – but only after an absence of more than two days.
Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance.

If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them.

Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.”

What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said.

In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America.

The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid.

In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white.
I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers.

“The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.”
In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born.

Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about.

Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves.

“The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’”

My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California.

title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives will spread lead over part of Iowa – what you need to know about the risks
paragraphs: The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice. According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation.” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.

The detonations were briefly delayed by the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026. And a federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued. It wasn’t immediately clear if the plan would be delayed again. The Justice Department argues that the permit isn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

With all the concern, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, about the risks people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.

This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-funded centers have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.

title: Preventable vision loss affects more than a billion people globally - and uneven access to care is the major culprit
paragraphs: Around the world, more than 1 billion people are living with vision loss in their daily lives. For many, this means they don’t have the glasses they need to see clearly. For others, conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration or diabetic eye disease have caused vision loss.
The burden of this problem is not shared equally – 55% of those experiencing vision loss are women and girls, 73% are ages 50 and older, and 90% live in low- and middle-income countries.

Age is the most important risk factor for vision loss. Since global populations are rapidly aging, the number of people experiencing vision loss is expected to increase to more than 1.7 billion by 2050.
So this public health threat is growing. Yet, it’s also almost entirely avoidable.

We are both population health researchers, and one of us is an opthamologist. We also lead the Michigan Sensory Health and Aging Research Collaborative at the University of Michigan, where we have spent years working to advance vision and eye health for underserved populations in the U.S. and globally. Recent developments give us hope that real progress is within reach.

Losing vision quite literally affects how people see the world, and it also increases their risk of other health issues, including falls, depression and even dementia. The risk of mortality is more than twice as high for adults living with vision loss.

The upside is that about 80% of vision loss can be reversed or prevented with timely detection and treatment. In fact, most cases can be fixed with eyeglasses or cataract surgery, two of the most cost-effective interventions in all of healthcare.

A recent report showed that eye care is not only important for health and well-being, but it is also a smart investment: Every dollar that low- and middle-income countries invest in eye health returns US$28 to their economies. This makes eye health easily one of the best deals in global health and development.

Back in 1999, the World Health Organization launched an initiative called VISION 2020: The Right to Sight. The aim was to draw attention and resources to vision and eye health problems, including those that would affect an aging global population.

More recently, in 2021, 193 United Nations member countries unanimously ratified a resolution calling on governments and international financial institutions to improve access to eye care and to provide the resources to make this possible.

In addition, this resolution acknowledged the central role of vision and eye health in achieving the U.N. sustainable development goals, a set of 17 ambitious aims, including universal access to food, clean water, education and work. Reframing vision and eye health as a development issue with a massive financial upside put the problem in front of people from a variety of sectors, such as education, labor and economics, and encouraged them to imagine how they could be a part of the solution.

In the five years since that resolution passed, the eye health sector has evolved some innovative strategies. For example, the new Vision Catalyst Fund brings together large-scale donors, nongovernmental organizations and local medical providers to test new approaches to paying for eye care and getting it to those most in need.

Another organization that has emerged to tackle avoidable vision loss is Peek Vision, a U.K.-based charity that began as a simple smartphone app. This app can be used by anyone with access to a smartphone to screen vision. So far, it has been used to screen more than 18 million people for vision loss and has connected more than 1.5 million to eye care. The organization is hoping to screen a million people per week by 2029.

In November 2026, the government of Antigua and Barbuda hosted the first-ever Global Summit for Eye Health, in collaboration with the governments of Nigeria, Guyana, Ireland and Bangladesh and the WHO. Policymakers, nongovernmental organizations, heads of state and global organizations such as the U.N., WHO and World Bank attended, with an eye toward a singular goal – ending avoidable sight loss worldwide.

The summit’s goal was to bring together key players from across the eye health sector. Governments and organizations are being asked to make forward-looking commitments toward accelerating progress. For example, 48 governments committed to embedding eye health in their national health systems, while health ministries, NGOs and eye hospitals have committed to providing cataract surgery and eyeglasses to tens of millions of people over the next few years.

The evidence to drive this investment is already there: Trials have shown that vision care for kids boosts educational outcomes. In middle-aged and older adults, research shows that an inexpensive pair of reading glasses boosts productivity and economic earnings in the agricultural, garment and artisan industries.

While low- and middle-income countries contend with the overwhelming majority of vision loss, the problem is also significant in the U.S., where an estimated 32.2 million people contend with vision loss.

Older adults are by far the most affected group. While they benefit from Medicare coverage for medical issues such as cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration, major gaps remain, including unequal access to advanced eye care and inconsistent coverage of eyeglasses by Medicare.

Under traditional Medicare, eyeglasses are covered only once in a beneficiary’s lifetime, following cataract surgery. Otherwise, glasses can be a large – and recurring – out-of-pocket expense. With a pair of glasses costing an average of US$200-$370 in the U.S., compared with roughly $35 in China or India, clear eyesight may be financially out of reach for many older Americans. Low-cost online retailers have helped to disrupt this market, but accessing glasses through those websites still requires internet access and a credit or debit card.

Older adults dealing with common issues such as cataracts or refractive error, which causes blurry vision, are at higher risk for all sorts of costly downstream health issues, including falls and dementia. Each year in the U.S., 2.3 million older adults wind up in the ER for a fall, and nearly 1 million are admitted to the hospital, costing the healthcare system about $20 billion. When it comes to dementia, the costs are even greater, at around $750 billion dollars per year.

Financing more comprehensive eye care for older Americans is actually in everyone’s best interest. In fact, every dollar that public programs such as Medicare invest in treating refractive error and cataracts in older Americans is likely to return $9 to the U.S. economy. Annually, this equates to around $23 billion. This return on investment comes in the form of increased economic productivity, medical cost savings, fewer falls and fewer people with dementia.

Being able to see clearly is essential to overall health and well-being. The data is clear, that regardless of a country’s level of wealth, it makes sense to put resources toward vision and eye health.

title: El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn
paragraphs: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, bringing lots of snow to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

I’m an avid skier and snow scientist at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be one of the strongest El Niños on record, let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns around the world.

It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was 2.5 C warmer (36.5 F, making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.

In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.
That pattern is almost exactly what’s being forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27. It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.

Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread destructive flooding in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. Fast-melting snow and days of heavy rain flooded the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.
Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered one of the lowest snow years on record for almost the entire western United States.

Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled. The two biggest – Lake Powell and Lake Mead – together supply water for about 40 million people and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.

The very low snowfall, as well as unusually warm midwinter temperatures that drove sublimation – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by record-high summer temperatures.
Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to alleviate a long-running drought that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.

In a positive sign, Lake Powell rose with the recent rains. Overall, the Super El Niño conditions being forecast for 2026-27 are expected to bring more than average rain and snow this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.
Snow scientists like me keep an eye on the South American winter in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.
Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.

South America saw a huge amount of snow, particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some areas like Portillo, the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.

The snow was a boon for Chile’s ski resorts. Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and extended its ski season, originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an explosion of spring flowers.

Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to pick up more moisture in this zone than usual, and this brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest.

If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.

title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
paragraphs: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people.

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.
“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.
One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.
My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion.

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460.
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.
Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
paragraphs: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor, I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher, I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two.

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism, which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “aesthetic” and “ethical” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote.

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires, not principles.
Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction: a pattern that we feel compelled to continue, despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction,” and whether love can become one, but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two.

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.
At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “a kind of despair,” rooted in estrangement from oneself, a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.
Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “Either/Or” and in “Works of Love,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.
Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love.”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote.

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves, a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.
